headline: Voyage Labs raises $12 million for a specialized AI travel assistant
author: Russell Brandom
content: Planning a trip is a favorite demo for personal AI assistants: you can try it with Muse, or with Gemini or half a dozen other choices. But while most pitches use travel-planning as part of a general-purpose agent pitch, a new startup from a Google Maps alum is betting that a specialized travel-planning agent can beat the competition. The company is called Voyage Labs, and on Tuesday it announced $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins, with participation from SignalFire and SV Angel. The company plans to use the funding to expand supplier partnerships and grow its engineering team. Voyage Labs’ flagship product is called Atlas, meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta. “People can use it to plan their and plan and book and manage their entire journey from the time they have an inspiration to the time they come back home,” says co-founder and CEO Manik Gupta. Atlas is designed to serve as an always-on assistant throughout the planning process, fielding ideas and doing research on every idea that’s raised. The long time horizon means Atlas can tailor recommendations based on weeks of conversation, while also monitoring real-time price fluctuations and ultimately booking flights and hotels. For the Voyage founders, it’s an ideal match between technology and use-case. “trip planning is a project that has its own lifecycle,” says Yogesh Jain, co-founder and CTO of the company. “You’re planning across days and weeks — so long-running agents as a technology matches that very well.” Travel assistants are already a crowded field, but Voyage will be starting with a lot of experience in the space. Gupta was previously the Director of Product Management for Google Maps, followed by four years as Chief Product Officer at Uber. headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B as it looks to take drug candidates to clinical trials
author: Ram Iyer
content: Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery platform that was spun out of Google’s DeepMind in 2021, has raised $5 billion in a Series C funding round as it seeks to take its drug candidates to clinical trials. The funding was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with new investor Andreessen Horowitz and other investors also participating. All of the company’s existing backers, including Alphabet’s venture divisions GV and Capital G, Thrive Capital, MGX, Temasek, and the UK Sovereign AI Fund, also invested. Isomorphic Labs builds an AI drug-design engine that uses a slew of simulation AI models that explore various areas of chemistry to help the company design drugs. The company, whose work builds on DeepMind’s breakthrough AlphaFold protein-folding AI model, said its program has yielded “positive preclinical results” in oncology and immunology. The lab has struck deals with pharma giants like Eli Lilly, Novartis, and Johnson & Johnson. The new funding, which comes on the heels of a $2.1 billion Series B round in May, will be used to continue developing its drug-design engine, as well as to foray into more types of medicine. The Series C is Isomorphic’s first fundraise since its founder and CEO, Demis Hassabis, left his position as head of DeepMind to focus on drug discovery, which also saw him moving into a chairman role at DeepMind. Hassabis and then-director of DeepMind John Jumper won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the lab’s work on AlphaFold, a system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins with nothing more than their genetic sequence. Isomorphic did not disclose its new valuation. Bloomberg reported earlier this month that the lab was looking to raise funding at a $50 billion valuation.

headline: Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding
author: Tim Fernholz
content: Science Corporation, the medical technology start-up founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post. Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech. Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain. Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialled for new conditions. Hodak announced that the device is now being trialled for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt’s disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt. With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the US. Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.
